description: Major muscle groups, agonist, antagonist and fixator roles in antagonistic muscle action.
content_html:
Why Muscles Work in Pairs

Muscles can only pull — they cannot push. Because of this, every joint in the body is controlled by at least two muscles that work in opposite directions. When one muscle contracts and shortens to produce movement, the opposing muscle relaxes and lengthens to allow that movement. This arrangement is called an antagonistic muscle pair. OCR also requires knowledge of a third muscle role — the fixator — which stabilises a nearby joint while movement occurs at another.

Major Muscles of the Body

At the shoulder, the deltoid forms the rounded cap of the shoulder. It is the prime mover for abduction of the arm (lifting it out to the side) and also contributes to flexion and extension. The trapezius is the large, diamond-shaped muscle that runs from the base of the skull down to the middle of the back. It elevates the shoulders, pulls the scapula back and assists head movement. The latissimus dorsi (‘lats’) is the broad muscle of the lower and mid-back, responsible for extension and adduction of the arm at the shoulder — powerful in swimming backstroke and rowing movements. The pectorals (chest muscles) lie across the front of the thorax and act as prime movers in horizontal adduction, such as in the press-up or front crawl pull phase.

At the elbow, the biceps sits on the front of the upper arm. During elbow flexion (the upward phase of a bicep curl), the biceps is the agonist (prime mover), contracting and shortening to pull the forearm up. On the back of the upper arm sits the triceps. During elbow flexion, the triceps acts as the antagonist, relaxing and lengthening to allow movement. The roles reverse completely during elbow extension (the downward phase of a press-up): the triceps becomes the agonist and the biceps becomes the antagonist. The deltoid acts as the fixator at the shoulder throughout the bicep curl, keeping the upper arm stable while the elbow moves.

The abdominals are the core muscles on the front of the trunk. They flex the spine, stabilise the pelvis during running and throwing, and are active in almost every sporting movement as a postural stabiliser and fixator.

At the hip and knee, two large muscle groups dominate. The quadriceps group (four muscles on the front of the thigh) is the prime mover for knee extension — straightening the knee. The hamstrings lie on the back of the thigh and are the prime mover for knee flexion (bending the knee). At the knee, the quadriceps and hamstrings form the classic antagonistic pair: quadriceps agonist during extension, hamstrings agonist during flexion. The gluteals are the large buttock muscles that drive hip extension — critical in sprinting and jumping.

At the ankle, the gastrocnemius runs from behind the knee down to the heel via the Achilles tendon. It is the prime mover for plantar flexion — pointing the toes down, as in sprinting push-off or jumping.

Key Fact

In the upward phase of a bicep curl: biceps = agonist (prime mover, contracts to flex the elbow), triceps = antagonist (relaxes and lengthens to allow the movement), deltoid = fixator (stabilises the shoulder joint so the upper arm stays still). In kicking (knee extension): quadriceps = agonist, hamstrings = antagonist.

Key Fact

The human body contains over 600 named muscles. Muscle fibres are packed with mitochondria — the organelles that produce ATP through aerobic respiration, supplying the energy needed for sustained muscular contraction during sport and exercise.

OCR explicitly requires three muscle roles — agonist, antagonist and fixator — while other boards only require two. Students who name only the agonist and antagonist will miss the fixator marks in OCR questions. A fixator is a muscle that holds a nearby body part still so that the prime mover can work efficiently. It does not produce the movement; it provides the stable base from which the movement occurs. In the bicep curl, the deltoid stabilises the shoulder joint throughout the exercise — without it, the shoulder would move and the elbow flexion would be inefficient. Always include the fixator and name the joint it stabilises.

A very common error in exams is to name a single muscle as ‘the agonist’ without specifying the joint, the direction of movement, or the antagonist and fixator. Mark schemes award marks for the complete picture: agonist named (1), antagonist named (1), fixator named and its role described (1), action described at the correct joint (1). Always frame answers as: “During elbow flexion, the biceps acts as the agonist (prime mover) while the triceps acts as the antagonist at the elbow joint. The deltoid acts as the fixator at the shoulder, stabilising the upper arm throughout the movement.”
exam_tip_html: For any OCR question asking about muscle roles during a movement, you must include all three roles: agonist (which muscle produces the movement), antagonist (which muscle relaxes to allow the movement), and fixator (which muscle stabilises the nearby joint). Missing the fixator is the most common reason students lose marks on this topic. On a 4-mark ‘Explain’ question, the mark scheme typically awards 1 mark for the agonist, 1 for the antagonist, 1 for the fixator with its joint, and 1 for accurately describing what each does in that specific movement. A common error is to say the antagonist ‘contracts’ — the antagonist relaxes and lengthens to allow the movement to occur. Make sure your sporting example specifies the phase of movement (e.g. ‘during the upward phase of a bicep curl’) to make it clear which muscle is the agonist at that moment.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • OCR requires three muscle roles: the agonist (prime mover that contracts to produce movement), the antagonist (which relaxes and lengthens to allow the movement), and the fixator (which stabilises a nearby joint so the prime mover can work efficiently). Always name all three in exam answers.
  • Key sporting pairs: biceps/triceps at the elbow (deltoid fixator), quadriceps/hamstrings at the knee, gluteals/hip flexors at the hip, gastrocnemius as prime mover for plantar flexion.
  • OCR’s extended muscle list includes deltoid, trapezius, latissimus dorsi, pectorals, biceps, triceps, abdominals, quadriceps, hamstrings, gluteals and gastrocnemius — know the location and primary action of each.

practice_questions.text: During a pull-up exercise, a gymnast bends her elbows to raise her body upward. Name the agonist muscle acting at the elbow joint during this upward phase.
Define the term 'fixator' and give one sporting example.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for definition: a muscle that stabilises a joint or body part to allow another muscle to contract effectively, holding a bone still while movement occurs elsewhere; 1 mark for a valid sporting example (e.g. the deltoid acts as the fixator at the shoulder during a bicep curl, keeping the upper arm stable while the elbow flexes / the abdominals act as fixators stabilising the pelvis during a sprint).

practice_questions.text: Describe the roles of the biceps, triceps and deltoid during the upward phase of a bicep curl.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for stating the biceps is the agonist, contracting to produce elbow flexion; 1 mark for stating the triceps is the antagonist, relaxing and lengthening to allow the movement; 1 mark for stating the deltoid is the fixator at the shoulder joint, stabilising the upper arm throughout the movement.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the quadriceps and hamstrings work as an antagonistic pair during a football kick, including what happens in both the upswing and the follow-through.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying the quadriceps as the agonist during knee extension (the upswing); 1 mark for explaining that the quadriceps contracts, shortening to straighten the knee and drive the foot towards the ball; 1 mark for identifying the hamstrings as the antagonist during the upswing, relaxing and lengthening to allow extension; 1 mark for explaining the role reversal on the follow-through: the hamstrings contract eccentrically (or as agonist) to decelerate the leg, acting as the prime mover for knee flexion to prevent over-extension and injury.

practice_questions.text: State two muscles from the OCR specification that are NOT in the biceps/triceps or quadriceps/hamstrings pairs, and state the primary action of each.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each correct muscle with its primary action. Accept any two from: deltoid (abduction of the arm at the shoulder), trapezius (elevation and retraction of the scapula / elevates shoulders), latissimus dorsi (extension and adduction of the arm at the shoulder), pectorals (horizontal adduction of the arm / adducts the arm across the chest), abdominals (flexion of the spine / stabilises the trunk and pelvis), gluteals (extension of the hip), gastrocnemius (plantar flexion at the ankle). Two identical or near-identical answers score 1 mark only.

practice_questions.text: A club-level badminton player performs a forehand smash. Analyse the roles of antagonistic muscle pairs and the fixator in producing this overhead striking action.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies at least two antagonistic pairs relevant to the smash (e.g. deltoid/latissimus dorsi at the shoulder; triceps/biceps at the elbow); each pair discussed in terms of agonist and antagonist roles anchored to specific phases of the smash; fixator named and its role explained (e.g. trapezius or abdominals as fixator stabilising the trunk or scapula); consistent sporting application throughout; technically accurate language.

Secure: Two pairs identified; mostly correct agonist/antagonist assignment; fixator mentioned; generally applied to the smash.

Developing: One pair discussed with development; or two pairs identified but fixator absent; sporting context present but superficial.

Emerging: Basic mention of agonist/antagonist with little development; fixator missing or incorrect; limited sporting application.

Acceptable content: at the shoulder, the deltoid (agonist) abducts and flexes to raise the arm; the latissimus dorsi and pectorals act as antagonists; at the elbow, the triceps (agonist) extends the elbow to produce the striking action; the biceps acts as the antagonist; the trapezius and abdominals act as fixators stabilising the scapula and trunk respectively.

knowledge_checks.q: Which muscle is the agonist during elbow flexion in the upward phase of a bicep curl?
In OCR, which is the third muscle role alongside agonist and antagonist?
During knee extension (kicking), the _____ is the agonist while the hamstrings act as the antagonist.
The _____ muscle on the back of the upper arm acts as the agonist during elbow extension.
Match each muscle to its primary action:
right: Abduction of the arm at the shoulder

flashcard_questions.q: What is an antagonistic muscle pair?
flashcard_questions.a: Two muscles working in opposite directions: the agonist contracts to produce movement, while the antagonist relaxes to allow it.

flashcard_questions.q: During elbow flexion, the biceps is the agonist. What is the antagonist?
flashcard_questions.a: Triceps — it relaxes and lengthens to allow the movement.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a fixator muscle and what does it do?
flashcard_questions.a: A muscle that stabilises a nearby joint, holding a body part still so the prime mover can work efficiently.

flashcard_questions.q: In a bicep curl, which muscle acts as the fixator and at which joint?
flashcard_questions.a: The deltoid acts as the fixator at the shoulder, keeping the upper arm stable throughout.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the primary action of the latissimus dorsi?
flashcard_questions.a: Extension and adduction of the arm at the shoulder — powerful in swimming and rowing.

flashcard_questions.q: Which muscle is the prime mover for plantar flexion at the ankle?
Which muscle group is the agonist for knee extension?
What is the deltoid's prime movement at the shoulder?
flashcard_questions.a: Abduction of the arm — lifting it out to the side.
Attach muscles to bones, transmitting contractile force to produce movement at the joint.

flashcard_questions.q: Which muscle on the back of the thigh is the agonist during knee flexion?
Name the large back muscle responsible for extension and adduction of the arm.
What is the trapezius and where is it located?
flashcard_questions.a: A large diamond-shaped muscle at the upper back that elevates the shoulders and retracts the scapula.

glossary_terms.definition: A pair of muscles that work in opposite directions across a joint: when the agonist contracts, the antagonist relaxes, and vice versa.
The prime mover muscle that contracts to produce a movement at a joint.
The muscle that relaxes and lengthens to allow the agonist to produce movement; the roles of agonist and antagonist reverse when the direction of movement reverses.
A muscle that stabilises a joint or body part to allow another muscle to contract effectively; it holds a bone still so the prime mover can work efficiently.
The triangular muscle capping the shoulder joint, responsible for abduction of the arm.
A large diamond-shaped muscle at the upper back that elevates, retracts and rotates the scapula.
The large fan-shaped muscle of the back responsible for extension and adduction of the arm at the shoulder.
A group of muscles on the back of the thigh that acts as the prime mover for knee flexion and assists hip extension.
The large muscle of the calf, acting as the prime mover for plantar flexion (pointing the foot downwards).

hero_image_caption: Muscles work in antagonistic pairs — understanding agonist, antagonist and fixator roles is essential for OCR PE.
narration_script: Muscles can only pull, not push. Every joint is therefore controlled by muscles working in opposite directions. When one muscle contracts, its partner relaxes. This is called antagonistic muscle action. OCR requires three muscle roles: the agonist, the antagonist and the fixator. The agonist is the prime mover that contracts to produce the movement. The antagonist relaxes and lengthens to allow the movement. The fixator stabilises a nearby joint so the prime mover can work efficiently. In the upward phase of a bicep curl, the biceps is the agonist at the elbow, the triceps is the antagonist, and the deltoid is the fixator at the shoulder. OCR specifies eleven muscles you must know: deltoid, trapezius, latissimus dorsi, pectorals, biceps, triceps, abdominals, quadriceps, hamstrings, gluteals and gastrocnemius. The quadriceps and hamstrings are the classic pair at the knee: quadriceps agonist during extension, hamstrings agonist during flexion. The gastrocnemius drives plantar flexion at the ankle. The trapezius elevates the shoulders. The latissimus dorsi extends and adducts the arm. Always name all three roles in your exam answers.
